scenes.narration: The family Benjamin Harrison came from matters more than the legends admit. Benjamin Harrison (August 20, 1833 – March 13, 1901) was the 23rd president of the United States, serving from 1889 to 1893. He was a member of the Harrison family of Virginia—a grandson of the ninth president, William Henry Harrison, and a great-grandson of Benjamin Harrison V, a Founding Father.

The first real success of Benjamin Harrison arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. A Union army veteran and a Republican, he defeated Democratic Party incumbent Grover Cleveland to win the presidency in the 1888 United States presidential election by winning the Electoral College while losing the popular vote. He was defeated by Cleveland in the 1892 United States presidential election, becoming the first president to be succeeded in office by his predecessor.

The last chapter of Benjamin Harrison was written long after the fame. Harrison was born on a farm by the Ohio River and graduated from Miami University in Oxford, Ohio. After moving to Indianapolis, he established himself as a prominent local attorney, Presbyterian church leader, and politician.

The whole life of Benjamin Harrison reads like a single decision repeated. During the American Civil War, he served in the Union Army as a colonel, and was confirmed by the U.S. In 1881, the Republican-controlled Indiana General Assembly elected Harrison to a six-year term in the Senate, where he served from 1881 to 1887.

Between the birth and the legend of Benjamin Harrison lie the years that actually decide it. Hallmarks of Harrison's administration were unprecedented economic legislation, including the McKinley Tariff, which imposed historic protective trade rates, and the Sherman Antitrust Act. Harrison also facilitated the creation of the national forest reserves through an amendment to the Land Revision Act of 1891.

The reputation of Benjamin Harrison was built in the middle, not at the edges. His proposals to secure federal education funding as well as voting rights enforcement for African Americans were unsuccessful. Due in large part to surplus revenues from the tariffs, federal spending reached $1 billion for the first time during his term.

Somebody like Benjamin Harrison should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. The spending issue in part led to the Republicans' defeat in the 1890 midterm elections. Cleveland defeated Harrison for reelection in 1892, due to the growing unpopularity of high tariffs and high federal spending.

The life of Benjamin Harrison begins far from where the story usually starts. In 1899, he represented Venezuela in its British Guiana boundary dispute with the United Kingdom. Harrison traveled to the court in Paris as part of the case and after a brief stay returned to Indianapolis.

Benjamin Harrison was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Harrison was born on August 20, 1833, in North Bend, Ohio, the second of Elizabeth Ramsey (Irwin) and John Scott Harrison's ten children. Harrison was of entirely English ancestry, all of his ancestors having emigrated to America during the early colonial period.

To understand where Benjamin Harrison ended up, start with where Benjamin Harrison began. Harrison was a grandson of U.S. president William Henry Harrison and a great-grandson of Benjamin Harrison V, a Virginia planter who signed the Declaration of Independence and succeeded Thomas Nelson Jr. as governor of Virginia. Harrison was seven years old when his grandfather was elected U.S. president, but he did not attend the inauguration.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Benjamin Harrison ran through years nobody filmed. John Scott Harrison, a two-term U.S. congressman from Ohio, spent much of his farm income on his children's education. Despite the family's modest resources, Harrison's boyhood was enjoyable, much of it spent outdoors fishing or hunting.

Each stage of the life of Benjamin Harrison made the next stage possible. Harrison's early schooling took place in a log cabin near his home, but his parents later arranged for a tutor to help him with college preparatory studies. Fourteen-year-old Benjamin and his older brother, Irwin, enrolled in Farmer's College near Cincinnati, Ohio, in 1847.

The people who knew Benjamin Harrison young describe someone already restless. He attended the college for two years and while there met his future wife, Caroline "Carrie" Lavinia Scott. She was a daughter of John Witherspoon Scott, who was the school's science professor and also a Presbyterian minister.

What Benjamin Harrison built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Harrison transferred to Miami University in Oxford, Ohio, in 1850, and graduated in 1852. He joined the Phi Delta Theta fraternity, which he used as a network for much of his life.

By the time Benjamin Harrison reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Classmates included John Alexander Anderson, who became a six-term U.S. congressman, and Whitelaw Reid, Harrison's vice presidential running mate in 1892. At Miami, Harrison was strongly influenced by history and political economy professor Robert Hamilton Bishop.

The rise of Benjamin Harrison was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. He also joined a Presbyterian church at college and, like his mother, became a lifelong Presbyterian. After his college graduation in 1852, Harrison studied law with Judge Bellamy Storer of Cincinnati, but before he completed his studies, he returned to Oxford, Ohio, to marry Caroline Scott on October 20, 1853.

Setbacks came early for Benjamin Harrison, and the response to them is the real story. The Harrisons had two children, Russell Benjamin Harrison and Mary "Mamie" Scott Harrison. Harrison and his wife returned to live at The Point, his father's farm in southwestern Ohio, while he finished his law studies.

The legacy of Benjamin Harrison outlived the circumstances that produced it. Harrison was admitted to the Ohio bar in early 1854, the same year he sold property he had inherited after the death of an aunt for $800 (equivalent to $28,667 in 2025), and used the funds to move with Caroline to Indianapolis, Indiana. Ray in 1854 and became a crier for the federal court in Indianapolis, for which he was paid $2.50 per day.

Few lives travel as far as that of Benjamin Harrison, and the distance is the point. Harrison became a founding member and first president of both the University Club, a private gentlemen's club in Indianapolis, and the Phi Delta Theta Alumni Club. Harrison and his wife became members and assumed leadership positions at Indianapolis's First Presbyterian Church.

The childhood of Benjamin Harrison contains the adult in small print. Having grown up in a Whig household, Harrison initially favored that party's politics, and joined the Republican Party shortly after its formation in 1856 and campaigned on behalf of Republican presidential candidate John C. In 1857 Harrison was elected Indianapolis city attorney, a position that paid an annual salary of $400 (equivalent to $13,821 in 2025).

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Benjamin Harrison — in that order. In 1858, Harrison entered into a law partnership with William Wallace to form the law office of Wallace and Harrison. Harrison was an active supporter of the Republican Party's platform and served as Republican State Committee's secretary.

The turning point in the life of Benjamin Harrison looked like a failure at the time. After Wallace, his law partner, was elected county clerk in 1860, Harrison established a new firm with William Fishback, Fishback and Harrison. The new partners worked together until Harrison entered the Union Army after the start of the American Civil War.

Every biography of Benjamin Harrison has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. In 1862, President Abraham Lincoln issued a call for more recruits for the Union Army; Harrison wanted to enlist, but worried about how to support his young family. While visiting Governor Oliver Morton, Harrison found him distressed over the shortage of men answering the latest call.

The education of Benjamin Harrison happened mostly outside any school. Morton asked Harrison if he could help recruit a regiment, although he would not ask him to serve. Morton offered him the command, but Harrison declined, as he had no military experience.

What Benjamin Harrison wanted at the start and what Benjamin Harrison got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Morton commissioned Harrison as a colonel on August 7, 1862, and the newly formed 70th Indiana was mustered into federal service on August 12, 1862. Once mustered, the regiment left Indiana to join the Union Army at Louisville, Kentucky.

The defining trait of Benjamin Harrison was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. For much of its first two years, the 70th Indiana performed reconnaissance duty and guarded railroads in Kentucky and Tennessee. Sherman's Atlanta campaign in the Army of the Cumberland and moved to the front lines.

Those who met Benjamin Harrison at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. On January 2, 1864, Harrison was promoted to command the 1st Brigade of the 1st Division of the XX Corps. He commanded the brigade at the battles of Resaca, Cassville, New Hope Church, Lost Mountain, Kennesaw Mountain, Marietta, Peachtree Creek, and Atlanta.

The private years of Benjamin Harrison explain the public decades better than any speech. When Sherman's main force began its March to the Sea, Harrison's brigade was transferred to the District of Etowah and participated in the Battle of Nashville. At the Battle of Resaca on May 15, 1864, Harrison faced Confederate Captain Max Corput's artillery battery, which occupied a position "some eighty yards in front of the main Confederate lines".

The family Benjamin Harrison came from matters more than the legends admit. Sherman, renewing his assault on the center of the Confederate lines begun the previous day, was halted by Corput's four-gun, parapet-protected artillery battery; the battery was well placed to bedevil the Union ranks, and became "the center of a furious struggle". Corput's artillery redoubt was fortified "with three infantry regiments in...rifle pits and four more regiments in the main trenches".

The first real success of Benjamin Harrison arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Leading the 70th Indiana Infantry Regiment, Harrison massed his troops in a ravine opposite Corput's position, along with the rest of Brigadier General William Thomas Ward's brigade. Harrison and his regiment, leading the assault, emerged from the ravine, advanced over the artillery parapet, overcame the Confederate gunners, and eliminated the threat.

The last chapter of Benjamin Harrison was written long after the fame. The battery was captured by hand-to-hand combat, and intense combat continued throughout the afternoon. Harrison's unit, now exposed, found itself immediately subject to intense gunfire from the main Confederate ranks and was forced to take cover.

The whole life of Benjamin Harrison reads like a single decision repeated. During the Battle of Peachtree Creek, on July 20, 1864, Harrison commanded his brigade against General W. In his report after the battle, Harrison wrote that "at one time during the fight", with his ammunition dangerously depleted, he sent his acting assistant inspector-general Captain Scott and others to cut "cartridge-boxes from the rebel dead within our lines" and distribute them to his soldiers.

Between the birth and the legend of Benjamin Harrison lie the years that actually decide it. According to Harrison's report, the losses from his brigade were "very slight" compared with those of Confederate forces. After the conclusion of the Atlanta Campaign on September 2, 1864, Harrison was among the initial Union forces to enter the surrendered city of Atlanta; General Sherman opined that Harrison served with "foresight, discipline and a fighting spirit".

The reputation of Benjamin Harrison was built in the middle, not at the edges. Harrison led the brigade at the Battle of Nashville in December, in a "decisive" action against the forces of General John Bell Hood. Notwithstanding his memorable military achievements and the praise he received for them, Harrison held a dim view of war.
